speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I understand you are a newborn presenting with respiratory distress; please tell me, did this distress start immediately after birth or was it delayed?

speaker: Patient
text: Newborn, born at 33 weeks of gestation. The newborn is presenting with respiratory distress 2 hours after birth. The mother had an uneventful pregnancy until premature onset of labor. There was no significant prenatal care history mentioned.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that information. Given the preterm status and the onset of distress within two hours, have you noticed any frothy fluid coming from the nose or mouth, or has the baby been breathing with significant effort?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Respiratory distress. I also have Grunting, Intercoastal and subcostal retractions, Peripheral cyanosis.

speaker: Doctor
text: The presence of grunting and retractions indicates significant work of breathing and likely surfactant deficiency. Given the history of prematurity and the physical exam findings, have you noticed the baby passing gas or stool? REQUEST TEST: Arterial_Blood_Gas

text: The blood gas confirms respiratory acidosis with hypoxia, which fits the picture of severe respiratory distress in a preterm infant. REQUEST IMAGES: Chest_XRay to look for air space disease or pneumothorax. Have you noticed any feeding difficulties or color changes other than cyanosis?

speaker: Doctor
text: The history of prematurity at 33 weeks combined with immediate onset of respiratory distress, grunting, retractions, and respiratory acidosis strongly suggests surfactant deficiency. REQUEST IMAGES: Chest_XRay to confirm ground-glass opacities typical of this condition. DIAGNOSIS READY: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS).
